name: journal-paul-on-holy-days.json
content:
What did Paul say about holy days? Two things, in two letters, and they pull against each other. To the Galatians he wrote in alarm that they were keeping days, months, seasons and years, and that he feared his work among them had been wasted.1 To the Romans he wrote that one person holds one day above another, another holds every day alike, and each should be fully convinced in his own mind.2

Today is Advent Sunday, the first day of the church's year in the West. It seems a fair day to ask how a man who said that much about the calendar came to have so many feasts kept in his name.

Galatians: the calendar as slavery

The Galatian passage is the sharper of the two. Paul reminds his readers that before they knew God they were enslaved to beings that are not gods by nature. Now that they know God, he asks, how can they turn back to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world and want to be enslaved again? Then comes the charge about days and seasons, and the fear that he laboured over them in vain.3

What were they keeping? The whole letter is an argument against Gentile believers taking up circumcision and the law of Moses, so most readers take the days and seasons to be the Sabbaths, new moons and festivals of the Torah. Some think pagan festivals are meant as well. The text does not settle it. What it does show is that Paul put the Galatians' observance of sacred time in the same sentence as their old slavery.

That is a hard thing to say of the feasts of the Torah. God gave Mūsā (ʿalayhi al-salām) the Sabbath and the pilgrim feasts, and the gospels show ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (ʿalayhi al-salām, peace be upon him) keeping them. Luke says his family went up to Jerusalem every year at Passover.4 John has him go up to the feast of Booths and teach in the Temple in the middle of it.5 He did not treat the days as a step back into slavery. How Paul set the covenant of Mūsā aside is the subject of [paulus_link slug="seven-doctrines-the-law-and-the-covenant" /].

Romans: the calendar as conscience

Romans is gentler. Paul is writing to a church he has never visited, with Jewish and Gentile members, and he wants them to stop judging each other over food and days. The one who observes the day, he says, observes it to the Lord.6 Neither side is to despise the other.

Look at what that does to a day God commanded. The Sabbath becomes a matter of private taste, as optional as eating meat. A commandment from Sinai is now an opinion, and a believer may keep it or drop it, provided he is sure of himself. The letters contain both of these Pauls, the one who calls the calendar slavery and the one who calls it a matter of conscience, and [paulus_link slug="the-letters-of-a-man" /] sets out why that matters for letters that are read as scripture.

Paul himself kept the Jewish year as a clock. He told the Corinthians he would stay at Ephesus until Pentecost.7 Acts has him sail from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and hurry to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost.8 And he turned the Passover into a figure for Christ. Christ, he says, is the Passover lamb already sacrificed, and the festival is to be kept with sincerity and truth.9

Colossians: a letter in his name

The verse quoted most often on this subject comes from Colossians. No one is to pass judgment on you over food and drink, a festival, a new moon or a Sabbath; these are a shadow of the things to come, and the substance belongs to Christ.10 Many scholars think Colossians was written in Paul's name after his death, and this site counts it among the letters the church received as his, not among the seven he certainly wrote. Its line on the calendar is close to Galatians, and it goes further: the feasts are now only shadows.

What the churches built

The churches that read these letters did not stay free of sacred days for long.

By the end of the second century they were already quarrelling over the date of Easter. The bishops of Asia kept it on the fourteenth of the Jewish month, whatever day of the week it fell, and Victor of Rome tried to cut them off for it.11 In 321 Constantine ordered courts and city trades to rest on "the venerable day of the Sun".12 By the late fifth century Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, had set fasts for the weeks between the feast of Saint Martin and Christmas, an early form of the season that begins today.13

Paul's own name entered the calendar too. Rome keeps the feast of Peter and Paul on 29 June, and the Western churches mark the conversion of Paul on 25 January. A man who told the Galatians that keeping seasons was a return to slavery has two days in the year named for him. Christmas, the feast at the end of Advent, has a history of its own, and the Journal of our sister site, Abrahamic Religions, takes up how it came to be set in December.

A Muslim reading

Islam has sacred time, and it is small and fixed. There is the Friday prayer, the fast of Ramaḍān and the two Eids. They come from revelation and the practice of the Prophet. The Qur'an asks of those who follow a religion God never ordained whether they have partners who laid it down for them, and it faults the earlier communities for taking their scholars and monks as lords beside God.14 A holy day is God's to give, and al-tawḥīd leaves no second lawgiver beside Him.15

Judged by that, Paul's letters did two things. They loosened the days God gave in the Torah, and they left the field open for the days the churches would later invent. Neither step came from ʿĪsā, who kept the feasts his people had been given. [paulus_link slug="paul-and-the-new-testament" /] follows how far the letters went in shaping the church that followed. Allāhu aʿlam.

Paul on holy days: questions readers ask

What does Galatians 4:10 mean?

Paul rebukes Gentile believers for observing days, months, seasons and years, and fears his work among them was wasted (Galatians 4:9–11). Most readers take him to mean the festivals of the law of Moses.

Did Paul say Christians do not need to keep the Sabbath?

In Romans he leaves the day to each believer's conscience (Romans 14:5–6). Colossians, a letter many scholars think was written in his name, says no one should judge believers over a Sabbath (Colossians 2:16).

Did Paul keep the Jewish festivals?

Acts has him plan his travel around Unleavened Bread and Pentecost (Acts 20:6, 16), and he planned to stay at Ephesus until Pentecost (1 Corinthians 16:8).

Did Paul celebrate Christmas?

No. No source from Paul's time mentions a feast of the birth, and his letters never give the date or place of ʿĪsā's birth.
